name: spectral-r1
context:
A NEW PLAN, PUT TO YOU BEFORE ANY OF IT IS BUILT. Two change sets: ten design changes drawn from external specification documents, and ten changes that REUSE code that already exists rather than writing it again. Nothing below is implemented yet.

─────────── WHAT THE EXTERNAL DOCUMENTS ACTUALLY SAY ───────────

I read four sources directly rather than summarising from memory.

(1) A band-law, called doc 26 in the corpus. It fixes a Z-ORDER BY TRUTH STATUS: forecast renders BENEATH ground truth, synthetic annotation renders ABOVE it. The stated reason is that a prediction drawn on top of a fact reads as a fact. It also binds forecast confidence to SATURATION, 'not size — a weak forecast is washed out, not smaller', and calls that the rule that matters most.

(2) Spec 34, an optical layer spec, which records that its own earlier draft VIOLATED that law by putting the infrared forecast above the board, and corrects it. Its central argument is a rank argument: a display emits a 3-vector per pixel, so mapping six information bands into colour is a linear map from R^6 to R^3 with a 3-dimensional null space — an infinite family of distinct game states produces identical pixels, and no palette tuning fixes a rank deficiency. Its escape is to stop using colour as the only carrier and to put each band on a separate perceptual axis: spatial frequency, orientation, temporal phase, achromatic envelope, glyph/topology, parallax. It cites a human-observer study (Hogervorst, Bijl & Toet 2007) in which three-channel colour mapping of hyperspectral data measured WORST of four presentation methods, and it flags that citation as thin — a tally of 4 — with the rank argument carrying the actual weight.

(3) Spec 34 also derives a rule I intend to adopt verbatim: NEVER ASK THE PLAYER TO COMPARE TWO MAGNITUDES. It comes from Thoen et al., Science 2014, where behavioural tests on mantis shrimp found wavelength discrimination of only 12-25 nm despite twelve photoreceptor classes, ruling out colour-opponent coding and leaving recognition-of-a-signature rather than discrimination-of-a-value. Every readout should answer 'is this line lit', quantised to four states.

(4) Spec 35, which specifies the two-row forecast grid the user asked for, and specifies it AS A COMPLIANCE FIX. A drop preview is a forecast; drawn over the board it breaks the band-law; drawn in a spatially separate strip above the board it complies, has no hit region, and lands where a phone thumb never covers. Row 1 is certain, row 2 is fallible, row 3 is never shown — depth capped at 2 by design, not by screen space. Spec 35's reason for the cap is economic: full drop-queue visibility converts a stochastic puzzle into a deterministic search problem, at which point the skill delta collapses into 'who wrote the better solver'.

─────────── A FALSIFICATION I FOUND WHILE READING OUR OWN CODE ───────────

Spec 35 §4.2 property 4 claims 'Row 1 is a pure function of (seed, tickIndex) via the counter-based RNG'. OUR ENGINE CANNOT HONOUR THAT CLAIM AS WRITTEN, and I only found out by reading lattice/round.ts rather than by trusting the spec.

Our refill draws from `state.rng`, a sequential stream. The number of draws consumed per turn is the number of EMPTY cells up to config.refill, which depends on what the player banked. Worse, a stagnation reshuffle rewrites all 36 cells and consumes 36 draws in one go. So the face that arrives on turn N is a function of the entire play history, not of (seed, N). A forecast grid built on the spec's stated property would be WRONG, and wrong in the specific way this project keeps catching: a claim inherited from a document instead of measured against the code.

The fix I propose reframes the forecast over the DRAW ORDINAL instead of the turn index. Faces are indexed by how many draws have been consumed, so the sequence is fixed by the seed and the only question is where in it we are. That makes row 1 genuinely certain, and it makes row 2 fallible FOR A REASON THIS ENGINE ACTUALLY HAS rather than an imported one: a reshuffle consumes 36 draws at once and slides the whole window, and whether a reshuffle fires depends on a board state that does not exist yet. That is honest fallibility emerging from our own mechanics.

─────────── SET A: TEN DESIGN CHANGES ───────────

A1. FORECAST STRIP, 6x2, SPATIALLY ABOVE AND NEVER Z-ABOVE. A separate 6-wide, 2-row strip over the board, no pointer events, no hit region, tapping it does nothing at all — not even a bounce, since a response would imply agency. Row 1 = the next 6 draws, certain. Row 2 = the 6 after, fallible. Row 3 never exists.

A2. ROW 2 CONFIDENCE AS WASHOUT TOWARD THE DECK VALUE, NEVER AS SIZE. Every row-2 cell is drawn at full size and washed toward GROUND until, at zero confidence, it is indistinguishable from an empty slot. This obeys the band-law's confidence rule while our palette stays achromatic-dark. Confidence is the integer probability that no reshuffle intervenes before that draw lands.

A3. FORECAST UNDER FACT IN Z-ORDER, EVERYWHERE ELSE TOO. Any on-board forecast (a charge-arrival hint) renders BENEATH the tile sprite, so only the halo past the tile edge is ever visible. A bloom occluded by its own tile reads as heat radiating from behind a solid object, which is what thermal emission looks like.

A4. FORECAST MAGNITUDE ON RADIUS, CONFIDENCE ON WASHOUT — TWO VARIABLES, TWO CARRIERS. The band-law forbids confidence-as-size; it does not forbid magnitude-as-size. Keeping them on separate carriers is what lets a tile be confidently cool or uncertainly hot.

A5. THE SYNTHETIC LAYER IS VISIBLY SYNTHETIC. Hard 1-device-pixel strokes, no anti-aliased gradients, values that snap between quantised states, a single-frame decode stutter when a channel mounts. It should look like something is COMPUTING, not glowing.

A6. NO READOUT MAY REQUIRE COMPARING TWO MAGNITUDES. Every overlay quantises to at most four states, and each state is nameable. This is a hard constraint on the visual search I intend to run, not a preference — the same geometric-mean fitness that has killed four previous designs, with a comparison-dependent encoding scoring zero.

A7. EVERY BAND MUST BE RECOVERABLE WITHOUT A LUMINANCE JUDGEMENT. Orientation, mark count, gap position and timing survive any tone curve; contrast is redundant only. Testable by rendering at reduced contrast and checking the state is still decodable.

A8. THE 4D ROTOR DRIVES THE PARALLAX PLATE. We already have engine/math/rotor4.ts with six rotation planes and projectTo3D. The synthetic overlay becomes a plate that shears against the board under a slow rotor in the XW plane, giving the annotation its own apparent depth. The rotor is the existing fixed-point one, so the shear is integer and reproducible.

A9. CHROMA IS RESERVED. Our palette is already near-achromatic (GROUND #080c12, CYAN #85e3ff, AMBER #ffce85). No overlay may introduce a saturated hue, because the six faces need the whole chroma budget. The forecast strip is therefore achromatic, distinguished by geometry.

A10. WRONG FORECASTS ARE VISIBLY CORRECTED. When a row-2 prediction resolves wrong, it is struck through rather than silently replaced. A forecast that quietly rewrites its own history is the slot-machine failure this project's reveal mechanic exists to invert. Under reduced-motion the correction is static.

─────────── SET B: TEN CHANGES THAT REUSE EXISTING CODE ───────────

I read libriopal/magentadice-cyancode at commit 8db018e. Its farkle-engine carries a discipline worth copying and, in four cases, code worth porting rather than rewriting.

B1. PORT THE CHAIN INDEX AS A PRECOMPUTED SCORE TABLE. chainIndex.ts encodes up to six dice into a dense base-6 integer (`(length-1)*46656 + base6`) and precomputes all 279,936 scores into an Int32Array once. Our chemistry mode currently re-derives the best rearrangement per selection. The same encode/decode/table shape applies directly to our selections and turns move enumeration into an array read.

B2. REUSE THE COUNTER-BASED CSPRNG FOR THE DRAW STREAM. csprng.ts is an HMAC-SHA256 stream keyed on (seed, counter). Adopting its counter discipline is exactly what makes the forecast honest — it is the fix for the falsification above, and it is already written and already tested.

B3. REUSE THE COMMIT-REVEAL TRIO VERBATIM. generateServerSeed / hashServerSeed / verifyServerSeed, including its constant-time comparison. Our lattice/commit.ts does the same job; reusing the exact function names and semantics makes our commitments checkable by anyone holding their verifier.

B4. COPY THE 'PORTED VERBATIM — DO NOT IMPROVE THIS FILE' HEADER CONVENTION. Every ported file in that repo carries a header naming its source repo, its source path, exactly what was changed (usually one import) and a line saying parity is the contract. We have oracles; we do not have provenance headers.

B5. COPY THE SACRED-CORE LOCK. That repo ships a `.ff-core-lock` listing files no agent may edit without authorisation — scorer, csprng, rtp config, event store. We have the same class of file (settlement, the Q16.16 domain, the append-only ledger) protected only by prose in comments.

B6. REUSE THE EXHAUSTIVE-NOT-GREEDY LESSON. Their scorer's header records that greedy scoring returned 1200 for two triplets where exhaustive returns 2500. Our chemistry `bestRearrangement` is a search; the same test shape — one input where greedy and exhaustive provably differ — belongs in verify-chem.

B7. REUSE THE SIGNATURE-NAMING PATTERN. `describeCombo` returns a NAME ('Two Triplets', 'Straight'), not a number, and the name is what the UI shows. Spec 34's evidence says signature-matching measured best of four presentations. Our chemistry mode already has formulas and names; the lattice mode shows bare integers and should show the shape it recognised.

B8. REUSE THE FOUR-AGENT HARNESS SHAPE. Spec 35 §5.2 runs RANDOM, GREEDY, HUMAN-CAL and MCTS-MAX over identical seed batteries and reports THE SPREAD BETWEEN THEM rather than the mean, on the argument that a harness reporting only means will pass a game a solver drains. We already have greedy and random reference players; we report means.

B9. REUSE HUMAN-CAL AS A NAMED BLOCKER, NOT A STUB. That spec marks its human-calibrated agent uncalibrated-until-playtest and refuses to report its output as a result. We should adopt the same discipline rather than fitting a placeholder distribution.

B10. REUSE THE INPUT-LOG-ONLY SUBMISSION CONTRACT. Their Entry submits an input log and never a score; the server replays it. Our heat-server already does exactly this. The reusable part is their explicit statement that the client's own figure is ADVISORY and a mismatch is a harvest artefact — we discard the mismatch instead of recording it.

─────────── WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING ───────────

I have not measured any of this. The 60fps requirement is unverified and I intend to measure it with a frame-time histogram rather than assert it. Spec 34's own confidence in 'four bands legible at once without fatigue' is 0.40, the lowest number in its table, and I am proposing to mount at most two.

questions.text: The forecast grid's row 2 is fallible because a stagnation reshuffle consumes 36 draws and slides the draw window. Is that a real epistemic uncertainty, or have I dressed up an implementation detail as a design virtue?

Spec 34's rank argument (six bands into a 3-vector has a 3-dimensional null space) is arithmetic. Does it actually support the design conclusion drawn from it, or does it only rule out a naive additive encoding that nobody proposed?
Set B proposes porting code from another repository. Which of B1-B10 is reuse in name only — where copying would import a decision that does not transfer to this codebase?
Showing a player the next 12 tokens raises the skill ceiling and also makes the board more solvable. Is a depth cap of 2 the right place to stop, and what evidence would settle it?
Name the single change in either set most likely to make the game WORSE, and say why.
